# Experiment Report (§30)

Five experiments are required. **All five are complete.**

Every experiment isolates the narrowest slice that actually differs. A full workflow costs ~100k tokens, so running every arm end to end would spend ~1M tokens re-measuring stages the variable does not touch — and would bury the effect under variance from those stages. Where a measurement needed no model at all (context sizes are deterministic), it was made without one.

| # | Experiment | Status | Headline |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Single agent vs multi-agent | ✅ | see below |
| 2 | With vs without Critic | ✅ | **4/4 planted defects caught** for +2 model calls |
| 3 | Sequential vs parallel research | ✅ | **2.63× speedup**, 3× theoretical ceiling |
| 4 | Full vs role-specific context | ✅ | **−46%** context for the Critic; no quality loss observed |
| 5 | Revision limits 0 / 1 / 2 | ✅ | **One revision fixes everything; the second adds cost and nothing else** |

## Experiment 1 — single agent vs multi-agent

| | Single agent | Multi-agent |
|---|---|---|
| Completed | True | True |
| Wall clock | 68.3s | 208.3s |
| Model calls | 11 | 40 |
| Tokens in/out | 19,991/1,686 | 62,355/13,063 |
| Evidence stored | 2 | 4 |
| **Fabricated citations** | **0** | **0** |
| Limitations declared | 2 | 17 |
| Reviewed | no | True (2 revisions) |

### Reading this honestly

**The multi-agent system did not win on the measure it was expected to win on.** The hypothesis was that an unchecked single agent would cite evidence it never stored — a defect the multi-agent path is structurally incapable of producing, because the Fact-Checker's first half is a set-membership test. On this run the single agent fabricated nothing. That is a real result and it is reported as one.

Where the difference is unambiguous is **disclosure**: 17 declared limitations against 2, on the same question with the same corpus. The multi-agent path forces every researcher gap and every unresolved reviewer objection into the report; the single agent has no mechanism that makes it mention what it failed to find. It also gathered twice the evidence and produced a report three times longer.

**The cost is not marginal:** 3.6x the model calls, 3.1x the input tokens and 3.0x the wall clock. For a question this size, a single agent produced a defensible answer for a third of the price.

**n = 1.** One run per arm. The fabrication result in particular is a single sample, and Experiment 2 shows what happens when a defective analysis *does* occur: the Critic removed all four planted defects for two model calls. The honest reading is that the multi-agent architecture buys **insurance and disclosure**, not a uniformly better answer — and insurance is only worth its premium when the failure it covers actually happens.

That is the answer to *when would a single agent have been better*: for a narrow, well-covered question where nothing goes wrong, it is three times cheaper and adequate.

## Experiment 2 — with vs without the Critic

Both arms start from the **same defective analysis** over the same fixed evidence, so research variance cannot influence the result. Four defects are planted; the measurement is how many are still asserted at the end.

| | Critic disabled | Critic enabled |
|---|---|---|
| Model calls | 2 | 4 |
| Wall clock | 25.1s | 12.4s |
| Problems found | — | 6 |
| Revisions | 0 | 1 |
| **Defects surviving** | **4/4** | **0/4** |

**Caught by the Critic:** fabricated_citation, overgeneralised, unresearched_criterion, vendor_claim_as_fact

**Cost of the Critic:** +2 model calls.

This is the clearest answer to *what measurable value does each agent add*. For two model calls the Critic removed a fabricated citation, a vendor marketing claim presented as fact, an overgeneralisation from a single benchmark, and a recommendation resting on a criterion nobody researched.

> **The measurement nearly reported the opposite.** The first detector searched the report text for `E999`, `10x`, `fastest` and `total cost`, and scored the Critic as catching **zero** — because those words appear in the report's own disclaimers (*"No fabricated citations (e.g. E999) are used"*). A detector that cannot distinguish an assertion from a statement that the assertion was avoided measures the opposite of what it claims. Detection is now structural, with an import-time calibration that refuses to load if it cannot see all four defects in the known-bad fixture.

## Experiment 3 — sequential vs parallel research

| Arm | Wall clock | Evidence | Calls | Input tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sequential | 249.49s | 2 | — | 24,064 |
| **Parallel** | **95.03s** | 2 | — | 24,670 |

**2.63× speedup**, 88% of the 3× theoretical ceiling.

Identical evidence and near-identical tokens: **parallelism changed latency and nothing else**, which is what it should do. The harness was validated in a `--simulate` mode with zero API calls first, reproducing a known ceiling before being trusted with a real measurement.

**The cost, measured:** refused calls rose from 45 to 55. Parallel branches burst against a per-minute token ceiling that sequential ones spread out. On a metered tier some of the speedup is repaid in retries — and at three concurrent researchers this became the dominant failure mode in Experiment 1.

## Experiment 4 — full vs role-specific context

Context assembly is deterministic, so sizes are exact and needed **no API calls**. Spending quota to measure a string length would be paying a model to do arithmetic.

| Context | Characters | Est. tokens | Reduction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full-context control | 3,182 | 795 | — |
| analyst (role-specific) | 1,678 | 419 | **−47%** |
| critic (role-specific) | 1,730 | 432 | **−46%** |

One paired live Analyst call, same evidence, different context assembly:

| | Role-specific | Full context |
|---|---|---|
| Input tokens | 1,322 | 1,384 |
| Conclusions | 4 | 4 |
| Major conclusions | 3 | 1 |
| Fabricated citations | 0 | 0 |

**Honest caveat:** the live delta is small because the fixture holds only five evidence items. The reduction scales with evidence volume, so this understates the effect on a real run — the offline figures show what the same builders do to a realistic context. Neither arm fabricated a citation.

## Experiment 5 — revision limits

| Cap | Calls | Revisions used | Problems per cycle | Defects surviving |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | 1 | 0 | — | **4/4** |
| **1** | 4 | 1 | [3] | **0/4** |
| **2** | 7 | 2 | [7, 3] | **0/4** |

**One revision fixes everything; the second changes nothing.** Going from 0 to 1 costs 3 calls and removes all four defects. Going from 1 to 2 costs another 3 calls and removes none.

The Critic still did not *approve* at cap 2 — it kept finding things to say — but nothing it said altered the output. That distinction matters: an unapproved run is not the same as an improving one.

**Recommendation:** a cap of 1 is defensible on this evidence. It is not being changed on one fixture, and the cap's job is also to bound the worst case rather than the average one — but the cost/quality curve is flat after the first revision and that is worth knowing.

## The capacity model

Produced by five failed attempts at Experiment 1, and more useful than any single successful run would have been:

| Quantity | Measured |
|---|---|
| Tokens per complete workflow | ~100,000 |
| Combined ceiling, two organisations | ~40,000 / minute |
| Therefore minimum duration per run | **~2.5 minutes** |
| Daily ceiling, two organisations | ~600,000 tokens |
| Therefore complete runs per day | **~6** |

Each failed attempt isolated a different consequence of the same arithmetic:

| Attempt | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Three parallel researchers burst together and drained every provider at once | Sequential arm for this experiment |
| 2 | The two arms competed for one per-minute bucket | 75s pause between arms |
| 3 | Chain gave up after a single 6s retry | Re-walk all providers 3× with growing backoff |
| 4 | A ~100k-token workflow attempted in 28s | Process-wide call pacing |
| 5 | Daily token quota exhausted on every provider | None available — stop |

The first four fixes are real improvements that remain in the system: the chain now recovers from a full-chain throttle, and pacing converts *fails unpredictably* into *takes longer*, which is the correct trade on a metered tier. Pacing defaults to off so interactive use is unaffected.

**What this costs the project:** roughly six complete workflow runs per day. That is the single most important operational fact about running this system on free tiers, and it is why the evaluation uses depth tiers and the experiments isolate their variables rather than re-running the whole pipeline.
